text: The directors asked their agent in the port to account for the missing cargo. His reply ran to nine pages and ended with a sentence somebody in the office underlined. “The whole of the pepper has been consumed by rats.” Eleven hundredweight of it.
strengths: the set-up makes the quotation land as the end of a long excuse
the underlining shows how the office read it without the narrator saying so
weaknesses: the closing fragment leans on the joke
a fragment after a quotation is a device the ear notices
spokenRhythm: Two medium sentences of set-up, the agent's own line, then a short fragment that lands the scale.
narrativeFunction: Lets the agent's excuse expose itself and points towards fraud without the narrator alleging it.
whyItWorks: The quotation is absurd on its own, and the single fragment after it gives the one fact that makes it impossible to believe. It is the kind of dry aside a person telling the story would make, and it arrives once, at the right moment.
whyItFails: A fragment after a quotation turns into a tic as quickly as any other device, and a run of them is a recognisable machine rhythm. It also tempts the narrator to answer every quotation with a punchline. Keep it for the one quotation that is already a joke, and give the number in a full sentence elsewhere.
rewrite: The directors asked their agent in the port to account for the missing cargo. His reply ran to nine pages and ended with a sentence somebody in the office underlined. “The whole of the pepper has been consumed by rats.” There had been eleven hundredweight of it.

text: The company's report to its shareholders said, “Not one life was lost.” In reality, the report was counting passengers. Four of the stokers drowned in the engine room.
strengths: the quotation is given in full before anything is said against it
the correction names exactly what the report left out
weaknesses: In reality is a debunking phrase that sounds like a presenter after its first use
spokenRhythm: A medium sentence ending on the quotation, a short turn, and a plain closing fact.
narrativeFunction: Sets an official claim against the record of who actually died.
whyItWorks: When the narration has to contradict a quoted claim, the listener needs a signal that the turn is coming, and said once, In reality is a plain one. The correction is precise, and the deaths are stated without adjectives.
whyItFails: In reality and The truth is are among the first habits a generated script repeats, and after the second one the film sounds like a debunking channel. Here the facts make the turn by themselves, so the phrase can usually go. Keep it only where the quotation is long enough that the listener needs help hearing the turn.
rewrite: The company's report to its shareholders said, “Not one life was lost.” The report was counting passengers. Four of the stokers drowned in the engine room.

text: After two warm winters, the ice merchant had borrowed against his house. In March his agent on the lake sent him a letter that reads like relief. “The ice is fourteen inches and clear as glass.”
strengths: the stakes are set before the quotation, so the listener knows why it matters
reads like admits that the relief is the narrator's reading
weaknesses: reads like relief tells the listener what to hear before they hear it
the phrase steps in front of a quotation that would carry the feeling on its own
spokenRhythm: A medium sentence of stakes, a medium sentence that frames the letter, and a short quotation to close.
narrativeFunction: Ends a run of bad winters with the agent's report on the new ice.
whyItWorks: Reads like is a fair, hedged way to point at the tone of a document, and it makes clear the reading is the narrator's. Once in a film, a light interpretation like this can help a listener who will never see the letter.
whyItFails: The borrowed house has already told the listener why the news matters, so naming the relief explains a feeling they would have had anyway. Done often, it becomes the narrator telling the audience how every quotation should sound, and with real people it slides into claiming to know their feelings. The rewrite sets the stakes and then lets the agent speak.
rewrite: After two warm winters, the ice merchant had borrowed against his house. In March his agent on the lake wrote to him, “The ice is fourteen inches and clear as glass.”
